nodes.name: Log-concave density
nodes.statement: A probability density function $p: \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}} \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ is \textit{log-concave} if its logarithm is concave, i.e., for any $x, y \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}} \times \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ and for any $\lambda \in [0, 1]$, \begin{align} p(\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) y) \geq p(x)^\lambda p(y)^{1-\lambda}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Log-concavity inequality
nodes.statement: p(\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) y) \geq p(x)^\lambda p(y)^{1-\lambda}.
nodes.label: eq:def_logconcave

nodes.name: Convex set
nodes.statement: A subset $K \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ is \textit{convex} if $\forall x, y \in K \times K, z \in [x, y] \implies z \in K$.
differentia: $\forall x, y \in K \times K, z \in [x, y] \implies z \in K$

nodes.name: Isoperimetric coefficient (Cheeger)
nodes.statement: The \textit{isoperimetric coefficient} $\psi(p)$ of a density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ is defined as \begin{align} \psi(p) := \inf_{S \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}} }\frac{p^+(\partial S)}{\min(p(S), p(S^c))} \end{align} where $p(S) = \int_{x \in S} p(x) dx$ and the boundary measure of the subset is \begin{align*} p^+(\partial S) := \underset{\epsilon \rightarrow 0^+}{\lim\inf}\ \frac{p\parenth{\braces{x: \mathbf{d}(x, S) \leq \epsilon}} - p(S)}{\epsilon}, \end{align*} where $\mathbf{d}(x, S)$ is the Euclidean distance between $x$ and the subset $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Cheeger isoperimetric coefficient: infimum over subsets of boundary measure over the smaller of the two measures.
also_stated_at: Given a distribution, the isoperimetric coefficient of a subset is the ratio of the measure of the subset boundary to the minimum of the measures of the subset and its complement. Taking the minimum of such ratios over all subsets defines the isoperimetric coefficient of the distribution, also called the Cheeger isoperimetric coefficient of the distribution.

nodes.name: Definition of psi(p)
nodes.statement: \psi(p) := \inf_{S \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}} }\frac{p^+(\partial S)}{\min(p(S), p(S^c))}
nodes.label: eq:def_isoperi

nodes.name: KLS conjecture
nodes.statement: There exists a universal constant $c$, such that for any log-concave density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$, we have \begin{align*} \psi(p) \geq \frac{c}{\sqrt{\spec{p}}}, \end{align*} where $\spec{p}$ is the spectral norm of the covariance matrix of $p$. In other words, $\spec{p} = \vecnorm{A}{2}$, where $A = \mathrm{Cov}_{X \sim p} (X)$ is the covariance matrix.
assumptions: for any log-concave density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$
nodes.statement_short: Cheeger constant of any log-concave density is at least a universal constant over the square root of its covariance spectral norm.
nodes.label: cj:main

nodes.name: Isotropic log-concave density
nodes.statement: We say a log-concave density is \textit{isotropic} if its mean $\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X\sim p} [X]$ equals to $0$ and its covariance $\mathrm{Cov}_{X\sim p}(X)$ equals to $\ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}$.

nodes.name: Original KLS bound
nodes.statement: \psi(p) \geq \frac{\log(2)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A}}}.
assumptions: for any log-concave density $p$ with covariance matrix $A$
nodes.label: eq:KLS_original_bound

nodes.name: Extension of KLS bound to log-concave densities
nodes.statement: The original KLS paper~\cite{kannan1995isoperimetric} only deals with uniform distributions over convex sets, but their proof techniques can be easily extended to show that the same results hold for all log-concave densities.

nodes.name: KLS bound in terms of dimension
nodes.statement: Remark that Equation~\eqref{eq:KLS_original_bound} implies $\psi(p) \geq \frac{\log(2)}{\ensuremath{d}^{1/2} \cdot \sqrt{\spec{p}}}$.

nodes.name: Lee-Vempala bound
nodes.statement: \psi(p) \geq \frac{c}{\parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^2}}^{1/4}}.
nodes.origin_citation: Lee & Vempala 2017 (Eldan's stochastic localization and the KLS hyperplane conjecture)
assumptions: for any log-concave density $p$ with covariance matrix $A$
nodes.label: eq:Lee_and_Vempala_bound

nodes.name: Lee-Vempala bound in terms of dimension
nodes.statement: It implies that $\psi(p) \geq \frac{c}{\ensuremath{d}^{1/4} \cdot \sqrt{\spec{p}}}$.

nodes.name: Thin-shell implies slicing (Eldan-Klartag)
nodes.statement: In terms of their connections to the KLS conjecture, Eldan and Klartag~\cite{eldan2011approximately} proved that the thin-shell conjecture implies Bourgain's slicing conjecture up to a universal constant factor.
conclusions: the thin-shell conjecture implies Bourgain's slicing conjecture up to a universal constant factor

nodes.name: KLS and thin-shell equivalence (Eldan)
nodes.statement: Later, Eldan~\cite{eldan2013thin} showed that the inverse of an lower bound of the isoperimetric coefficient is equivalent to an upper bound of the thin-shell constant in the thin-shell conjecture.
conclusions: the inverse of an lower bound of the isoperimetric coefficient is equivalent to an upper bound of the thin-shell constant in the thin-shell conjecture

nodes.name: KLS bounds imply thin-shell and slicing bounds
nodes.statement: Combining these two results, we have that an lower bound in the KLS conjecture implies upper bounds in the thin-shell conjecture and in Bourgain's slicing conjecture.
conclusions: an lower bound in the KLS conjecture implies upper bounds in the thin-shell conjecture and in Bourgain's slicing conjecture

nodes.name: Almost constant lower bound in the KLS conjecture
nodes.statement: There exists a universal constant $c$ such that for any log-concave density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ and any integer $\ell \geq 1$, we have \begin{align} \psi(p) \geq \frac{1}{\brackets{c \cdot \ell \parenth{\log(\ensuremath{d})+1}}^{\ell/2} \ensuremath{d}^{16/\ell} \cdot \sqrt{\spec{p}}} \end{align} where $\spec{p}$ is the spectral norm of the covariance matrix of $p$.
assumptions: for any log-concave density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$
any integer $\ell \geq 1$
nodes.statement_short: Isoperimetric coefficient of any log-concave density is at least $1/([c\ell(\log d+1)]^{\ell/2} d^{16/\ell}\sqrt{\rho(p)})$ for every integer $\ell$.
nodes.label: thm:main_KLS

nodes.name: psi_d: worst-case normalized isoperimetric coefficient
nodes.statement: For this, we define the supremum of the product of the isoperimetric coefficient and the square-root of its spectral norm over all log-concave densities in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ with compact support: \begin{align} \psi_{\ensuremath{d}} = \inf_{\text{ \shortstack{log-concave density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ \\ with compact support}}} \psi(p) \sqrt{\spec{p}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\psi_d$ is the infimum of $\psi(p)\sqrt{\rho(p)}$ over compactly supported log-concave densities in $\mathbb{R}^d$.

nodes.statement: Suppose that $\psi_k \geq \frac{1}{\alpha k^\beta}$ for all $k \leq \ensuremath{d}$ for some $0 \leq \beta \leq \frac{1}{2}$ and $\alpha \geq 1$, take $q = \lceil \frac{1}{\beta} \rceil + 1$, there exists a universal constant $c$ such that we have \begin{align*} \psi_{\ensuremath{d}} \geq \frac{1}{c \cdot q^{1/2} \alpha \log(\ensuremath{d})^{1/2} \ensuremath{d}^{\beta - \beta / (8q) }}. \end{align*}

take $q = \lceil \frac{1}{\beta} \rceil + 1$

nodes.name: Eldan's stochastic localization SDE
nodes.statement: Given a log-concave density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ with covariance matrix $A$, we define the following stochastic differential equation (SDE) \begin{align} dc_t &= C_t^{1/2}dW_t + C_t \mu_t dt,\quad c_0 = 0,\\ dB_t &= C_t dt,\quad B_0 = 0, \notag \end{align} where $W_t$ is the Wiener process, the matrix $C_t$, the density $p_t$, the mean $\mu_t$ and the covariance $A_t$ are defined as follows \begin{align} C_t &= A^{-1}, \\ p_t(x) &= \frac{e^{c_t^\top x - \frac{1}{2}x^\top B_t x} p(x)}{\int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}} e^{c_t ^\top x - \frac{1}{2}y^\top B_t y} p(y) dy}, \text{for $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$},\\ \mu_t &= \int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}} x p_t(x)dx, \\ A_t &= \int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}} \parenth{x - \mu_t}\parenth{x - \mu_t} p_t(x) dx, \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Stochastic localization: SDE for $(c_t,B_t)$ tilting $p$ by $e^{c_t^\top x - x^\top B_t x/2}$, with mean $\mu_t$ and covariance $A_t$ of $p_t$.

nodes.statement: Given a density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ with compact support with covariance $A$ and $A$ is invertible, then the SDE~\eqref{eq:def_SDE_ctBt} is well defined and it has a unique solution on the time interval $[0, T]$, for any time $T > 0$. nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 2 (stochastic localization strategy)
nodes.statement: Before we dive into the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:induction_isoperi}, we discuss how the stochastic localization scheme allows us to control the boundary measure of a subset. First, according to the concavity of the isoperimetric profile (Theorem 2.8 in Sternberg and Zumbrun~\cite{sternberg1999connectivity} or Theorem 1.8 in Milman~\cite{milman2009role}), it is sufficient to consider subsets of measure $1/2$ in the definition of the isoperimetric coefficient in Equation~\eqref{eq:def_isoperi}. Second, the density $p_t$ is log-concave and it is more log-concave than the Gaussian density proportional to $e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^\top B_t x}$. It can be shown via the KLS localization lemma~\cite{kannan1995isoperimetric} that a density which is more log-concave than a Gaussian has an isoperimetric coefficient lower bound that depends on the covariance of the Gaussian (see e.g. Theorem 2.7 in Ledoux~\cite{ledoux2001concentration} or Theorem 4.4 in Cousins and Vempala~\cite{cousins2014cubic}). Third, given an initial subset $E$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ with measure $p(E) = \frac{1}{2}$, using the martingale property of $p_t(E)$, we observe that \begin{align*} p(\partial E) &= \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}} \brackets{p_t(\partial E)} \\ & \stackrel{(i)}{\geq} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}\brackets{\frac{1}{2}\vecnorm{B_t^{-1}}{2}^{-1/2} \min \parenth{p_t(E), p_t(E^c)}} \\ & \stackrel{(ii)}{\geq} \frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\vecnorm{B_t^{-1}}{2}^{-1/2} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}( \frac{1}{4}\leq p_t(E) \leq \frac{3}{4})\\ & = \frac{1}{4}\vecnorm{B_t^{-1}}{2}^{-1/2} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}( \frac{1}{4}\leq p_t(E) \leq \frac{3}{4}) \cdot \min\braces{p(E), p(E^c)}. \end{align*} Inequality (i) uses the isoperimetric inequality for a log-concave density which is more log-concave than a Gaussian density proportional to $e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^\top B_t x}$ \cite{ledoux2001concentration,cousins2014cubic}. Inequality (ii) uses the fact that $p_t(E)$ is nonnegative. Based on the above observation, the high level idea of the proof requires two main steps: \begin{itemize} \item There exists some time $t > 0$, such that the Gaussian component $\frac{1}{2}x^\top B_t x$ of the density $p_t$ is large enough, so that we can apply the known isoperimetric inequality for densities more log-concave than a Gaussian. \item We need to control the quantity $p_t(E)$ so that the obtained isoperimetric inequality at time $t$ can be related back to that at time 0. \end{itemize} The first step is obvious since our construction explicitly enforces the density $p_t$ to have a Gaussian component $\frac{1}{2}x^\top B_t x$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:def_SDE_parameters}. Then the remaining question is whether we can run the SDE long enough to make the Gaussian component large enough while still keeping $p_t(E)$ to be the same order as $p(E) = \frac{1}{2}$ with large probability.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: reduce to sets of measure 1/2, bound boundary measure via Gaussian-isoperimetry of $p_t$, and control $p_t(E)$ to transfer back to time 0.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:induction_isoperi} follows the strategy described after Lemma~\ref{lem:existence_SDE_solution}. We make the arguments rigorous here. We consider a log-concave density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ with compact support. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the covariance matrix $A$ of the density $p$ is invertible. Otherwise, the density $p$ is degenerate and we can instead prove the results in a lower dimension. According to the concavity of the isoperimetric profile (Theorem 2.8 in Sternberg and Zumbrun~\cite{sternberg1999connectivity} or Theorem 1.8 in Milman~\cite{milman2009role}), it is sufficient to consider subsets of measure $1/2$ in the definition of isoperimetric coefficient~\eqref{eq:def_isoperi}. Given an initial subset $E$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ with $p(E) = \frac{1}{2}$, use the martingale property of $p_{T_2}(E)$, we have \begin{align*} p(\partial E) &= \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}} \brackets{p_{T_2}(\partial E)} \\ & \stackrel{(i)}{\geq} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}\brackets{\frac{1}{2}\vecnorm{B_{T_2}^{-1}}{2}^{-1/2} \min \parenth{p_{T_2}(E), p_{T_2}(E^c)}} \\ & \stackrel{(ii)}{\geq} \frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\vecnorm{B_{T_2}^{-1}}{2}^{-1/2} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}( \frac{1}{4}\leq p_{T_2}(E) \leq \frac{3}{4})\\ & = \frac{1}{4}\vecnorm{B_{T_2}^{-1}}{2}^{-1/2} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}}( \frac{1}{4}\leq p_{T_2}(E) \leq \frac{3}{4}) \cdot \min\braces{p(E), p(E^c)} \\ &\stackrel{(iii)}{\geq} \frac{1}{8}\vecnorm{B_{T_2}^{-1}}{2}^{-1/2} \cdot \min\braces{p(E), p(E^c)} \\ &\stackrel{(iv)}{=} \frac{1}{8}T_2^{1/2}\vecnorm{A}{2}^{-1/2} \cdot \min\braces{p(E), p(E^c)}. \end{align*} Inequality (i) uses the isoperimetric inequality for a log-concave density which is more log-concave than a Gaussian density proportional to $e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^\top B_t x}$ (see e.g. Theorem 2.7 in Ledoux~\cite{ledoux2001concentration} or Theorem 4.4 in Cousins and Vempala~\cite{cousins2014cubic}). Inequality (ii) follows from the fact that $p_t(E)$ is nonnegative. (iii) follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:g_control} and Lemma~\ref{lem:isoperi_implies_A_control} (for $\ensuremath{d} \geq 3$). (iv) follows from the construction that $B_t = t A^{-1}$. We conclude the proof since $T_2$ is taken as $\frac{1}{ c \cdot q \alpha^2\log(\ensuremath{d}) \ensuremath{d}^{2\beta - \beta/(4q)}}$ with $c$ as a constant. The above proof only works for $\ensuremath{d} \geq 3$. It is easy to verify that Lemma~\ref{lem:induction_isoperi} still holds for the case for $\ensuremath{d} = 1, 2$ from the original KLS bound in Equation~\eqref{eq:KLS_original_bound}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:main_lemma_KLS} consists of applying Lemma~\ref{lem:induction_isoperi} recursively. We define \begin{align*} \alpha_1 = 4, \beta_1 = \frac{1}{2}. \end{align*} For $\ell \geq 1$, we define $\alpha_\ell$ and $\beta_\ell$ recursively as follows: \begin{align} \alpha_{\ell+1} &= 2c \cdot \alpha_\ell \beta_\ell^{-1/2}, \notag \\ \beta_{\ell+1} &= \beta_\ell - \beta_\ell^2/16, \end{align} where $c$ is the constant in Lemma~\ref{lem:induction_isoperi}. It is not difficult to show by induction that $\alpha_\ell$ and $\beta_\ell$ satisfy \begin{align} \frac{1}{\ell+1} &\leq \beta_\ell \leq \frac{16}{\ell} \notag \\ \alpha_\ell &\leq \parenth{4c^2 \ell}^{\ell/2}. \end{align} We start with a known bound from the original KLS paper~\cite{kannan1995isoperimetric} \begin{align*} \psi_{\ensuremath{d}} \geq \frac{1}{\alpha_1 \ensuremath{d}^{\beta_1}},\quad \forall \ensuremath{d} \geq 1. \end{align*} In the induction, suppose that we have \begin{align*} \psi_{\ensuremath{d}} \geq \frac{1}{\alpha_\ell \parenth{\log(\ensuremath{d})+1}^{\ell/2} \ensuremath{d}^{\beta_\ell}},\quad \forall \ensuremath{d} \geq 1. \end{align*} From the above inequality, we obtain for any $1 \leq k \leq \ensuremath{d}$, \begin{align*} \psi_k \geq \frac{1}{\alpha_\ell' k^\beta_\ell}, \end{align*} with $\alpha_\ell' = \alpha_\ell \parenth{\log(\ensuremath{d}) +1}^{\ell/2}$. Using the above lower bounds for $\psi_k$, we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:induction_isoperi}. For integer $\ell+1$, we have \begin{align*} \psi_{\ensuremath{d}} &\stackrel{(i)}{\geq} \frac{1}{c \cdot q^{1/2} \alpha_\ell \parenth{\log(\ensuremath{d})+1}^{l/2} \log(\ensuremath{d})^{1/2} \ensuremath{d}^{\beta_\ell - \beta_\ell / (8q) }}\\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{\geq} \frac{1}{2c \cdot \alpha_\ell \beta_\ell^{-1/2} \parenth{\log(\ensuremath{d})+1}^{(l+1)/2} \ensuremath{d}^{\beta_\ell - \beta_\ell^2 / 16 }} \\ &= \frac{1}{\alpha_{\ell+1} \parenth{\log(\ensuremath{d})+1}^{(\ell+1)/2} \ensuremath{d}^{\beta_{\ell+1}}} \end{align*} where inequality (i) follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:induction_isoperi}, inequality (ii) follows from $q \leq \frac{2}{\beta}$ and the last equality follows from the definition of $\alpha_\ell$ and $\beta_\ell$. We conclude Lemma~\ref{lem:main_lemma_KLS} using the $\alpha_\ell$ and $\beta_\ell$ bounds in Equation~\eqref{eq:alpha_beta_l_bound}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: To derive Theorem~\ref{thm:main_KLS} from Lemma~\ref{lem:main_lemma_KLS}, it is sufficient to show that for any log-concave density $p$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$, most of its probability measure is on a compact support. Let $\mu$ be the mean of the density $p$. Since $r \mapsto p(\mathbb{B}\parenth{\mu, r}^c)$ is an non-increasing function of $r$ with limit $0$ at $\infty$, there exists a radius $R > 0$, such that $p(\mathbb{B}\parenth{\mu, R}^c) \leq 0.2$. Note that it is possible to get a better bound via e.g. log-concave concentration bounds from Paouris~\cite{paouris2006concentration}, but knowing the existence of such radius $R$ is sufficient for the proof here. Denote $B = \mathbb{B}\parenth{\mu, R}$. Then $p(B^c)\leq 0.2$. Let $\varrho$ be the density obtained by truncating $p$ on the ball $B$. Then $\varrho$ is log-concave and it has compact support. For a subset $E \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ of measure such that $p(E) = \frac{1}{2}$, we have \begin{align*} p(\partial E) &\geq \varrho(\partial E) p(B) \\ &\geq \psi(\varrho) \min\parenth{\varrho(E), \varrho(E^c)} p(B) \\ &= \psi(\varrho) \min\parenth{p(E \cap B), p(B \cap E^c)} \\ &\geq \psi(\varrho) \min\parenth{p(E) - p(B^c), p(E^c) - p(B^c)} \\ &\geq \frac{1}{2} \psi(\varrho) \min\parenth{p(E), p(E^c)}. \end{align*} The last inequality follows because $p(E^c) - p(B^c) \geq 0.5 - 0.2 \geq \frac{1}{4}$. Since it is sufficient to consider subsets of measure 1/2 in the definition of the isoperimetric coefficient~\cite{sternberg1999connectivity,milman2009role}, we conclude that the isoperimetric coefficient of $p$ is lower bounded by half of that of $\varrho$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:main_lemma_KLS} for the isoperimetric coefficient of $\varrho$, we obtain Theorem~\ref{thm:main_KLS}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:potentwo_derivative_bound}:} We first prove the bound on $\vecnorm{v_t}{2}$, where \begin{align*} v_t = q \int A^{-1/2} \parenth{x-\mu_t} \parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} \parenth{Q_t}^{q-1} A^{-1/2} \parenth{x-\mu_t} p_t(x) dx. \end{align*} Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:tensor_vector_bound} and knowing the covariance of $p_t$ is $A_t$, we obtain \begin{align*} \vecnorm{v_t}{2} &\leq 16 q \vecnorm{A_t^{1/2} A^{-1} A_t^{1/2}}{2}^{1/2} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A_t^{1/2} A^{-1/2} Q_t^{q-1} A^{-1/2} A_t^{1/2}} \\ &\stackrel{(i)}{=} 16 q \vecnorm{A_t^{1/2} A^{-1} A_t^{1/2}}{2}^{1/2} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{Q_t^{q}} \\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{=} 16 q \vecnorm{Q_t}{2}^{1/2} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{Q_t^{q}} \\ &\stackrel{(iii)}{\leq} 16 q \brackets{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{Q_t^{q}}}^{1+1/(2q)}. \end{align*} Equality (i) uses the definition of $Q_t = A^{-1/2} A_t A^{-1/2}$. Equality (ii) uses the fact that $\vecnorm{MM^\top}{2} = \vecnorm{M^\top M}{2}$ for any square matrix $M \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d} \times \ensuremath{d}}$. Inequality (iii) uses that $\vecnorm{M}{2} \leq \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{M^q}^{1/q}$ for any positive semi-definite matrix $M$. Next, we bound $\delta_t$ in two ways. We can ignore the negative term in $\delta_t$ to obtain the following: \begin{align} \delta_t &\leq \frac{q}{2} \sum_{a = 0}^{q-2} \int \int \parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} Q_t^{a} A^{-1/2} \parenth{y-\mu_t} \notag \\ &\cdot \parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} Q_t^{q-2-a} A^{-1/2} \parenth{y-\mu_t} \parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1} \parenth{y-\mu_t} p_t(x) p_t(y) dx dy \notag \\ &= \frac{q}{2} \sum_{a = 0}^{q-2} \mathcal{T}_{\varrho_t}(Q_t^{a}, Q_t^{q-2-a}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}), \end{align} where $\varrho_t$ is the density of linear-transformed random variable $A^{-1/2}\parenth{X-\mu_t}$ for $X$ drawn from $p_t$ and $\mu_t$ is the mean of $p_t$. $\varrho_t$ is still log-concave since any linear transformation of a log-concave density is log-concave (see e.g. Saumard and Wellner~\cite{saumard2014log}). $\varrho_t$ has covariance $A^{-1/2} A_t A^{-1/2}$, which is also $Q_t$. For $a \in \braces{0, \cdots, q-2}$, we have \begin{align*} \mathcal{T}_{\varrho_t}(Q_t^{a}, Q_t^{q-2-a}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}) &\stackrel{(i)}{\leq} \mathcal{T}_{\varrho_t}(Q_t^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}) \\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} 128 \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) \ensuremath{d}^{2\beta - 1/q} \brackets{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{Q_t^q}}^{1+1/q}. \end{align*} Inequality (i) follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ttensor_swap}. Inequality (ii) follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ttensor_A_isoperimetric_bound}. Since there are $q-1$ terms in the sum, we conclude the first part of the bound for $\delta_t$. On the other hand, since $p_t$ is more log-concave than the Gaussian density proportional to $e^{-\frac{t}{2} (x-\mu_t)^\top A^{-1} (x-\mu_t)}$, $\varrho_t$ is more log-concave than the Gaussian density proportional to $e^{-\frac{t}{2} x^\top x}$. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:poten_h_bound}:} The function $h$ has the following derivatives \begin{align*} \frac{d h}{d a} = \frac{1}{q} \parenth{a + 1}^{-1/q - 1}, \frac{d^2 h}{da^2} = -\frac{q+1}{q^2} \parenth{a + 1}^{-1/q - 2}. \end{align*} Using It\^o's formula, we obtain \begin{align*} d h(\Gamma_t) &= \left.\frac{d h}{d a}\right|_{\Gamma_t} d\Gamma_t + \frac{1}{2} \left.\frac{d^2 h}{d a^2}\right|_{\Gamma_t} d\brackets{\Gamma}_t \\ &= \frac{1}{q (\Gamma_t+1)^{1/q+1}} d\Gamma_t - \frac{1}{2} \frac{q+1}{q^2 (\Gamma_t+1)^{1/q+2}} \vecnorm{v_t}{2}^2 dt \\ &\leq \frac{1}{q (\Gamma_t+1)^{1/q+1}} d\Gamma_t \\ &\stackrel{(i)}{\leq} 64 q \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) \ensuremath{d}^{2\beta-1/q} dt + \frac{v_t^\top dW_t}{q \parenth{\Gamma_t + 1}^{1/q+1}}, \end{align*} where inequality (i) plugs in the bounds in Lemma~\ref{lem:potentwo_derivative_bound}. Define a martingale $Y_t$ such that \begin{align*} dY_t = \frac{v_t^\top dW_t}{q \parenth{\Gamma_t + 1}^{1/q+1}}, \end{align*} with $Y_0 = 0$. According to the $\vecnorm{v_t}{2}$ upper bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:potentwo_derivative_bound}, we have \begin{align*} \vecnorm{\frac{1}{q \parenth{\Gamma_t + 1}^{1 + 1/q}}v_t}{2}^2 &\leq 256. \end{align*} Hence the martingale $Y_t$ is well-defined. According to the Dambis, Dubins-Schwarz theorem (see e.g. Revuz and Yor~\cite{revuz2013continuous} Section V.1 Theorem 1.7), there exits a Wiener process $\tilde{W}_t$ such that $Y_t$ has the same distribution as $\tilde{W}_{[Y]_t}$. Then we have for any $\gamma > 0$, \begin{align} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}} \parenth{\max_{t \in [0, T]} Y_t \geq \gamma} \leq \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}} \parenth{\max_{t \in [0, T]} \tilde{W}_{256t} \geq \gamma} \leq \exp\parenth{-\frac{\gamma^2}{512 T}}. \end{align} Set $T = \frac{1}{32768 q \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) d^{2\beta}}$ and $\Psi = \frac{1}{2} \parenth{\ensuremath{d}+1}^{-1/q}$. Observe that $\Gamma_0 = \ensuremath{d}$ and as a result $h(\Gamma_0) = -\parenth{\ensuremath{d}+1}^{-1/q}$. Then we have \begin{align*} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}} \parenth{\max_{t \in [0, T]} h(\Gamma_t) \geq -\Psi} &\leq \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}} \parenth{\max_{t \in [0, T]} Y_t \geq -\Psi + \parenth{\ensuremath{d}+1}^{-1/q} - \int_0^T 64q \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) d^{2\beta - 1/q} dt }\\ &\stackrel{(i)}{\leq} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{P}}} \parenth{\max_{t \in [0, T]} Y_t \geq \frac{\Psi}{4}} \\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} \exp\parenth{-\frac{\Psi^2}{8192T}} \\ &\stackrel{(iii)}{\leq} \exp\parenth{-\frac{2}{3} q \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) \ensuremath{d}^{2\beta - 2/q}} \notag \\ &\stackrel{(iv)}{<} \frac{3}{10}. \end{align*} Inequality (i) follows from the choice of $T$. (ii) uses Equation~\eqref{eq:Y_t_tail_bound}. (iii) follows by plugging in $\Psi = \frac{1}{2}\parenth{\ensuremath{d}+1}^{-1/q}$ and $3^q \ensuremath{d}^2 \geq 2^q (\ensuremath{d} + 1)^2$. (iv) follows from $\beta q \geq 1$, $\ensuremath{d} \geq 3$, $q\geq 2$ and $3^{-4/3} < 0.3$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace_DeltaDelta_bound}:} For the first part, we have \begin{align*} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta P \Delta} = \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X \sim p} X^\top \Delta P X \cdot X ^\top v. \end{align*} Since $\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X\sim p} X^\top v = 0$, we can subtract the mean of the first term $X^\top \Delta P X$ without changing the value of $\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta P \Delta} $. Then \begin{align*} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta P \Delta} &= \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X\sim p} \brackets{\parenth{X^\top \Delta P X - \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{Y \sim p} Y ^\top \Delta P Y} \cdot X ^\top v} \\ &\stackrel{(i)}{\leq} \parenth{\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X\sim p}(X^\top v)^2}^{1/2} \parenth{\mathrm{Var}_{X \sim p }\parenth{X ^\top \Delta P X}}^{1/2} \\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} 2 \psi_{\min(2r, \ensuremath{d})}^{-1} \parenth{\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X \sim p} \vecnorm{\Delta P X + P^\top \Delta^\top X}{2}^2}^{1/2} \\ & \leq 4 \psi_{\min(2r, \ensuremath{d})}^{-1} \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta P \Delta}}^{1/2}. \end{align*} Inequality (i) follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Inequality (ii) follows from the fact that $\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X\sim p}(X^\top v)^2 = 1$ as $p$ is isotropic and that the inverse Poincar\'e constant is upper bounded by twice of inverse of the squared isoperimetric coefficient (also known as Cheeger's inequality~\cite{maz1960classes,cheeger1969lower} or Theorem 1.1 in Milman~\cite{milman2009role}). The matrix $\Delta P + P^\top \Delta$ has rank at most $\min(2r, \ensuremath{d})$. Rearranging the terms in the above equation, we conclude the first part of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace_DeltaDelta_bound}. For the second part, we write the matrix $A$ in its eigenvalue decomposition and group the terms by eigenvalues. We have \begin{align*} A = \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i v_i v_i^\top = \sum_{j=1}^J A_j + B, \end{align*} where $A_i$ has eigenvalues between the interval $(\vecnorm{A}{2} e^{i-1} /\ensuremath{d}, \vecnorm{A}{2} e^{i} /\ensuremath{d}]$ and $B$ has eigenvalues smaller than or equal to $\vecnorm{A}{2}/\ensuremath{d}$. Because the intervals have right bounds increasing exponentially, we have $J = \lceil \log(\ensuremath{d}) \rceil$. Let $P_i$ be the orthogonal projection matrix formed by the eigenvectors in $A_i$. Then we have \begin{align} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta A_i \Delta} \leq \vecnorm{A_i}{2} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta P_i \Delta} \stackrel{(i)}{\leq} 16 \vecnorm{A_i}{2} \psi^{-2}_{\min(2 \text{rank}(A_i), \ensuremath{d})} \stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} 16 \alpha^2 \vecnorm{A_i}{2} \cdot \parenth{2 \text{rank}(A_i)}^{2\beta}, \end{align} where inequality (i) follows from the first part of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace_DeltaDelta_bound} and inequality (ii) follows from the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace_DeltaDelta_bound}. Similarly for matrix $B$, we have \begin{align} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta B \Delta} \stackrel{(i)}{\leq} 16 \alpha^2 \vecnorm{B}{2} \parenth{2\text{rank}(B)}^{2\beta} \stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} 32 \alpha^2 \vecnorm{A}{2}, \end{align} where inequality (i) follows from the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace_DeltaDelta_bound} and inequality (ii) follows from the fact that $\vecnorm{B}{2} \leq \vecnorm{A}{2}/d$ and $2\beta \leq 1$. Putting the bounds~\eqref{eq:trace_DeltaDelta_Ai_bound} and~\eqref{eq:trace_DeltaDelta_B_bound} together, we have \begin{align*} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta A \Delta} &= \sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta A_j\Delta} + \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta B \Delta} \\ &\leq 16 \alpha^2 \parenth{\sum_{j=1}^J \vecnorm{A_j}{2} \cdot \parenth{2\text{rank}(A_j)}^{2\beta} + 2\vecnorm{A}{2}} \\ &\stackrel{(i)}{\leq} 16 \alpha^2 \brackets{\parenth{\sum_{j=1}^J \vecnorm{A_j}{2}^{1/(2\beta)} \cdot \parenth{2\text{rank}(A_j)}}^{2\beta} \cdot \parenth{J}^{1-2\beta} + 2\vecnorm{A}{2}}\\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} 16 \alpha^2\brackets{\parenth{2 e \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^{1/(2\beta)}}}^{2\beta} \cdot \parenth{J}^{1-2\beta} + 2 \vecnorm{A}{2}} \\ &\leq 128 \alpha^2 \log(\ensuremath{d}) \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^{1/(2\beta)}}}^{2\beta}. \end{align*} Inequality (i) follows from Holder's inequality and inequality (ii) follows from the fact that $\vecnorm{A_j}{2}^{1/2\beta} \text{rank}(A_j) \leq e \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A_{j}^{1/2\beta}}$ due to the construction of $A_j$. This concludes the second part of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace_DeltaDelta_bound}.

Then through a change of variable, we have \begin{align*} &\mathcal{T}_p \parenth{A^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} \\ =& \int\int (x-\mu)^\top A^{q-2} (y-\mu) \cdot (x-\mu)^\top (y-\mu) \cdot (x-\mu) ^\top (y-\mu) p(x) p(y) dx dy \\ =& \int\int \parenth{x^\top A^{q-1} y} (x^\top A y) (x ^\top A y) \varrho(x) \varrho(y) dx dy \\ \leq& \int\int \parenth{x^\top A^{q} y} (x^\top A y) (x ^\top y) \varrho(x) \varrho(y) dx dy \\ =& \mathcal{T}_\varrho \parenth{A^{q}, A, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}}, \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ttensor_swap}. $A^q$ is positive semi-definite and we write down its eigenvalue decomposition $A^q = \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i v_i v_i ^\top$ with $\lambda_i \geq 0$. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 11
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:ttensor_oneoverT_bound}:} Without loss of generality, we can assume that the density $p$ has mean $0$. Its covariance matrix $A$ is positive semi-definite and invertible. We can write down its eigenvalue decomposition as follows $A = \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i v_i v_i^\top$ with $\lambda_i > 0$ and $v_i$ are eigenvectors with norm $1$. Then $A^{q}$ has an eigenvalue decomposition with the same eigenvectors $A^q = \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^q v_i v_i^\top$. Define $\Delta_i = \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X \sim p} (X^\top A^{-1/2}v_i) X X ^\top$, then \begin{align} \mathcal{T}_p\parenth{A^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} &= \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X, Y \sim p} \parenth{X^\top A^{q-2} Y} (X^\top Y) (X ^\top Y) \notag \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q-1} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta_i \Delta_i}. \end{align} Next we bound the terms $\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta_i \Delta_i}$. We have \begin{align*} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta_i \Delta_i} &= \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X \sim p} \parenth{X ^\top A^{-1/2} v_i} X^\top \Delta_i X \\ &\stackrel{(i)}{=} \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X \sim p} \parenth{X ^\top A^{-1/2} v_i} \parenth{X^\top \Delta_i X - \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{Y \sim p} \brackets{Y^\top \Delta_i Y}} \\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} \parenth{\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X \sim p} \parenth{X ^\top A^{-1/2} v_i}^2 }^{1/2} \parenth{\mathrm{Var}\parenth{X ^\top \Delta_i X}}^{1/2} \\ & \stackrel{(iii)}{=} \parenth{\mathrm{Var}_{X \sim p}\parenth{X ^\top \Delta_i X}}^{1/2} \\ &\stackrel{(iv)}{\leq} \parenth{\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X \sim p} \frac{1}{\tau} \vecnorm{\Delta_i X + \Delta_i X}{2}^2}^{1/2} \\ &\stackrel{(v)}{\leq} \parenth{\frac{4}{\tau} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A \Delta_i \Delta_i}}^{1/2}. \end{align*} Equality (i) is because $\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X \sim p} X = 0$. Inequality (ii) follows from Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Equality (iii) follows from the definition of the covariance matrix $\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X\sim p} XX^\top = A$. Inequality (iv) follows from the Brascamp-Lieb inequality (or Hessian Poincar\'e, see Theorem 4.1 in Brascamp and Lieb~\cite{brascamp2002extensions}) together with the assumption that $p$ is more log-concave than $\ensuremath{\mathcal{N}}(0, \frac{1}{\tau}\ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}})$. Plugging the bounds of the terms $\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta_i \Delta_i}$ into Equation~\eqref{eq:ttensor_oneoverT_first_step}, we obtain \begin{align*} \mathcal{T}_p\parenth{A^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} &= \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q-1} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta_i \Delta_i} \\ &\leq \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q-1} \parenth{\frac{4}{\tau} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A \Delta_i \Delta_i}}^{1/2} \\ &\stackrel{(i)}{\leq} \frac{2}{\tau^{1/2}} \parenth{\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q}}^{1/2} \parenth{\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q-2} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A \Delta_i \Delta_i} }^{1/2} \\ &= \frac{2}{\tau^{1/2}} \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^q}}^{1/2} \parenth{\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X, Y \sim p} \parenth{X^\top A^{q-3} Y} (X^\top A Y) (X ^\top Y) }^{1/2} \\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} \frac{2}{\tau^{1/2}} \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^q}}^{1/2} \parenth{\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X, Y \sim p} \parenth{X^\top A^{q-2} Y} (X^\top Y) (X ^\top Y) }^{1/2} \\ &= \frac{2}{\tau^{1/2}} \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^q}}^{1/2} \brackets{\mathcal{T}_p\parenth{A^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} }^{1/2}. \end{align*} Inequality (i) follows from Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. For $q \geq 3$, inequality (ii) follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ttensor_swap}. From the above equation, after rearranging the terms, we obtain \begin{align*} \mathcal{T}_p\parenth{A^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} \leq \frac{4}{\tau} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^q}. \end{align*}

nodes.statement: Plugging the bounds of the terms $\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta_i \Delta_i}$ into Equation~\eqref{eq:ttensor_oneoverT_first_step}, we obtain \begin{align*} \mathcal{T}_p\parenth{A^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} &= \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q-1} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{\Delta_i \Delta_i} \\ &\leq \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q-1} \parenth{\frac{4}{\tau} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A \Delta_i \Delta_i}}^{1/2} \\ &\stackrel{(i)}{\leq} \frac{2}{\tau^{1/2}} \parenth{\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q}}^{1/2} \parenth{\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \lambda_i^{q-2} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A \Delta_i \Delta_i} }^{1/2} \\ &= \frac{2}{\tau^{1/2}} \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^q}}^{1/2} \parenth{\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X, Y \sim p} \parenth{X^\top A^{q-3} Y} (X^\top A Y) (X ^\top Y) }^{1/2} \\ &\stackrel{(ii)}{\leq} \frac{2}{\tau^{1/2}} \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^q}}^{1/2} \parenth{\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X, Y \sim p} \parenth{X^\top A^{q-2} Y} (X^\top Y) (X ^\top Y) }^{1/2} \\ &= \frac{2}{\tau^{1/2}} \parenth{\mathrm{Tr}\parenth{A^q}}^{1/2} \brackets{\mathcal{T}_p\parenth{A^{q-2}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}, \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}} }^{1/2}. \end{align*} Inequality (i) follows from Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the density $p$ has mean $0$. For $i \in  races{1, \cdots, \ensuremath{d}}$, we define $\Delta_i = \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X\sim p} B^{1/2} X X ^	op B^{1/2} X^	op C^{1/2} e_i$ where $e_i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$ is the vector with $i$-th coordinate 1 and 0 elsewhere. We have $\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} e_i e_i ^	op = \ensuremath{\mathbb{I}}_{\ensuremath{d}}$. We can rewrite the tensor on the left hand side as a sum of traces.  egin{align} &\mathcal{T}_{p}(B^{1/2}A^\delta B^{1/2}, B^{1/2}A^{1-\delta}B^{1/2}, C) 
otag \ =& \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{X, Y \sim p} X^	op B^{1/2}A^\delta B^{1/2} Y \cdot X^	op B^{1/2}A^{1-\delta}B^{1/2} Y \cdot X ^	op C Y

nodes.name: Prove the trace inequality
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the trace inequality in Equation~\eqref{eq:trace_ineq_lieb_thirring}. Without loss of generality, we can assume $G$ is diagonal. Hence, we have \begin{align*} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{G^\delta F G^{1-\delta} F} &= \sum_{i = 1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \sum_{j = 1}^{\ensuremath{d}} G_{ii}^\delta G_{jj}^{1-\delta} F_{ij}^2 \\ &\leq \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \sum_{j=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \parenth{\delta G_{ii} + (1-\delta) G_{jj}} F_{ij}^2 \\ &= \delta \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \sum_{j=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} G_{ii} F_{ij}^2 + (1-\delta) \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \sum_{j=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} G_{jj} F_{ij}^2 \\ &= \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{G F^2}, \end{align*} where the inequality follows from Jensen's inequality and the fact that the logarithm function is concave (or the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means).

nodes.name: Rewrite the SDE
nodes.statement: We can rewrite the stochastic differential equation~\eqref{eq:def_SDE_ctBt} as follows to make the dependency clear: \begin{align*} dc_t &= A^{-1/2} dW_t + A^{-1} \mu\parenth{c_t, B_t} dt\\ dB_t &= A^{-1} dt, \end{align*} where \begin{align*} \mu(c, B) &= \int x \varrho(c, B, x) dx, \\ \varrho(c, B, x) &= \frac{e^{c^\top x - \frac{1}{2}x^\top B x} p(x)}{\int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}} e^{c ^\top x - \frac{1}{2}y^\top B y} p(y) dy}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Lipschitz coefficients; SDE existence and uniqueness theorem
nodes.statement: Since $p$ has a compact support, given $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}$, $\varrho(\cdot, \cdot, x)$ as a function of $(c, B)$ is Lipschitz in $c$ and $B$. Similarly, $\mu$ is also Lipschitz in $c$ and $B$. Consequently, $A^{-1/2}$, $A \mu(c_t, B_t)$ and $A^{-1}$ are all bounded and Lipschitz on $c_t$ and $B_t$ on the compact support. Applying the existence and uniqueness theorem of SDE solutions (Theorem 5.2 in {\O}ksendal~\cite{oksendal2003stochastic}), we show that the SDE solution exists and is unique on the time interval $[0, T]$ for any $T > 0$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives
nodes.statement_short: Lipschitz coefficients; SDE existence and uniqueness theorem

nodes.name: Derivative of $p_t$
nodes.statement: Next, we derive the derivative of $p_t$. Define \begin{align*} G_t(x) &= e^{c_t^\top x - \frac{1}{2} x^\top B_t x} p(x), \\ V_t & = \int G_t(x) dx. \end{align*} Then $p_t(x)$ can be written as $\frac{G_t(x)}{V_t}$. Let $S_t(x)$ denote the quadratic variation of the process $c_t^\top x$. We have \begin{align*} d S_t(x) = x^\top A^{-1} x dt. \end{align*} Using It\^o's formula, we have \begin{align*} dG_t(x) &= \parenth{x^\top (dc_t) - \frac{1}{2} x^\top dB_t x + \frac{1}{2} dS_t} G_t(x) \\ &= \parenth{x^\top A^{-1/2}dW_t + x^\top A^{-1} \mu_t dt} G_t(x), \\ dV_t &= \int dG_t(x) dx = V_t \parenth{\mu_t^\top A^{-1/2}dW_t + \mu_t^\top A^{-1} \mu_t dt}. \end{align*} Using It\^o's formula on the inverse of $V_t$, we have \begin{align*} d V_t^{-1} &= -\frac{dV_t}{V_t^2} + \frac{d \brackets{V}_t} {V_t^3} \\ &= - V_t^{-1} \brackets{\mu_t^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t + \mu_t^\top A^{-1} \mu_t dt} + V_t^{-1} \mu_t^\top A^{-1} \mu_t dt \\ &= - V_t^{-1} \mu_t^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t. \end{align*} Using It\^o's formula on $p_t$, with the above derivatives, we obtain \begin{align*} dp_t(x) &= d \parenth{V_t^{-1} G_t(x)} \\ &= \parenth{G_t(x) dV_t^{-1} + V_t^{-1}dG_t(x) + d\brackets{V^{-1}, G(x)}_t} \\ &= \parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t p_t(x). \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Define $G_t$, $V_t$, $S_t$
nodes.statement: Next, we derive the derivative of $p_t$. Define \begin{align*} G_t(x) &= e^{c_t^\top x - \frac{1}{2} x^\top B_t x} p(x), \\ V_t & = \int G_t(x) dx. \end{align*} Then $p_t(x)$ can be written as $\frac{G_t(x)}{V_t}$. Let $S_t(x)$ denote the quadratic variation of the process $c_t^\top x$. We have \begin{align*} d S_t(x) = x^\top A^{-1} x dt. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Ito for $G_t$ and $V_t$
nodes.statement: Using It\^o's formula, we have \begin{align*} dG_t(x) &= \parenth{x^\top (dc_t) - \frac{1}{2} x^\top dB_t x + \frac{1}{2} dS_t} G_t(x) \\ &= \parenth{x^\top A^{-1/2}dW_t + x^\top A^{-1} \mu_t dt} G_t(x), \\ dV_t &= \int dG_t(x) dx = V_t \parenth{\mu_t^\top A^{-1/2}dW_t + \mu_t^\top A^{-1} \mu_t dt}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Ito for $V_t^{-1}$
nodes.statement: Using It\^o's formula on the inverse of $V_t$, we have \begin{align*} d V_t^{-1} &= -\frac{dV_t}{V_t^2} + \frac{d \brackets{V}_t} {V_t^3} \\ &= - V_t^{-1} \brackets{\mu_t^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t + \mu_t^\top A^{-1} \mu_t dt} + V_t^{-1} \mu_t^\top A^{-1} \mu_t dt \\ &= - V_t^{-1} \mu_t^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Combine to get $dp_t$
nodes.statement: Using It\^o's formula on $p_t$, with the above derivatives, we obtain \begin{align*} dp_t(x) &= d \parenth{V_t^{-1} G_t(x)} \\ &= \parenth{G_t(x) dV_t^{-1} + V_t^{-1}dG_t(x) + d\brackets{V^{-1}, G(x)}_t} \\ &= \parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t p_t(x). \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Derivative of $A_t$
nodes.statement: Then we derive the derivative of $A_t$. By the definition of $A_t$, we have \begin{align*} A_t = \int \parenth{x - \mu_t} \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx, \end{align*} where $\mu_t = \int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}} x p_t(x) dx$. Using It\^o's formula on $\mu_t$, we obtain \begin{align*} d\mu_t &= \int x d p_t(x) dx \\ &= \int x (x- \mu_t)^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t p_t(x) dx \\ &= \int (x - \mu_t) (x- \mu_t)^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t dx\\ &= A_t A^{-1/2} dW_t. \end{align*} Using It\^o's formula on $A_t$ and viewing it as a function of $\mu_t$ and $p_t$, we obtain \begin{align*} dA_t =& \int \parenth{x - \mu_t}\parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top dp_t(x) dx - \int d\mu_t\parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx - \int \parenth{x - \mu_t}\parenth{d\mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx \\ &-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \int \parenth{x - \mu_t} d\brackets{\mu_t^\top, p_t(x)}_t dx - \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \int d\brackets{\mu_t, p_t(x)}_t \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top dx \\ &+ \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 d\brackets{\mu_t, \mu_t^\top}_t \int p_t(x) dx. \end{align*} We observe that $\int d\mu_t\parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx = 0$ and $\int \parenth{x - \mu_t}\parenth{d\mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx = 0$. Then, \begin{align*} d\brackets{\mu_t^\top, p_t(x)}_t &= \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top A^{-1} A_t p_t(x) dt,\\ d\brackets{\mu_t, p_t(x)}_t &= A_t A^{-1} \parenth{x - \mu_t} p_t(x) dt, \\ d\brackets{\mu_t, \mu_t}_t &= A_t A^{-1} A_t dt. \end{align*} Combining all the terms together, we have \begin{align*} dA_t = \int \parenth{x - \mu_t} \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top \parenth{\parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t} p_t(x) dx - A_tA^{-1} A_t dt. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Recall $A_t$ and $\mu_t$
nodes.statement: Then we derive the derivative of $A_t$. By the definition of $A_t$, we have \begin{align*} A_t = \int \parenth{x - \mu_t} \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx, \end{align*} where $\mu_t = \int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d}}} x p_t(x) dx$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Ito for $\mu_t$
nodes.statement: Using It\^o's formula on $\mu_t$, we obtain \begin{align*} d\mu_t &= \int x d p_t(x) dx \\ &= \int x (x- \mu_t)^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t p_t(x) dx \\ &= \int (x - \mu_t) (x- \mu_t)^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t dx\\ &= A_t A^{-1/2} dW_t. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Ito for $A_t$
nodes.statement: Using It\^o's formula on $A_t$ and viewing it as a function of $\mu_t$ and $p_t$, we obtain \begin{align*} dA_t =& \int \parenth{x - \mu_t}\parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top dp_t(x) dx - \int d\mu_t\parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx - \int \parenth{x - \mu_t}\parenth{d\mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx \\ &-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \int \parenth{x - \mu_t} d\brackets{\mu_t^\top, p_t(x)}_t dx - \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \int d\brackets{\mu_t, p_t(x)}_t \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top dx \\ &+ \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 d\brackets{\mu_t, \mu_t^\top}_t \int p_t(x) dx. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Cross-variation terms
nodes.statement: We observe that $\int d\mu_t\parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx = 0$ and $\int \parenth{x - \mu_t}\parenth{d\mu_t}^\top p_t(x) dx = 0$. Then, \begin{align*} d\brackets{\mu_t^\top, p_t(x)}_t &= \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top A^{-1} A_t p_t(x) dt,\\ d\brackets{\mu_t, p_t(x)}_t &= A_t A^{-1} \parenth{x - \mu_t} p_t(x) dt, \\ d\brackets{\mu_t, \mu_t}_t &= A_t A^{-1} A_t dt. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Combine to get $dA_t$
nodes.statement: Combining all the terms together, we have \begin{align*} dA_t = \int \parenth{x - \mu_t} \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top \parenth{\parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t} p_t(x) dx - A_tA^{-1} A_t dt. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Derivative of $\Gamma_t$
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Derivatives of $\Gamma(X)=\mathrm{Tr}(X^q)$
nodes.statement: Finally, we derive the derivative of $\Gamma_t$. Define the function $\Gamma: \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{\ensuremath{d} \times \ensuremath{d}} \mapsto \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ as $\Gamma(X) = \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{X^q}$. The first-order and second-order derivatives of $\Gamma$ are given by \begin{align*} \left.\frac{\partial \Gamma}{\partial X}\right|_{H} = q \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{ X^{q-1} H}, \left.\frac{\partial^2 \Gamma}{\partial X \partial X}\right|_{H_1, H_2} = q \sum_{a=0}^{q-2} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{X^a H_2 X^{q-2-a} H_1}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Ito formula for $\Gamma_t$
nodes.statement: Using the above derivatives and It\^o's formula, we obtain \begin{align} d\Gamma_t = d \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{Q_t^q} = q \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{ Q_t^{q-1} d Q_t} + \frac{q}{2} \sum_{a = 0}^{q-2} \sum_{i,j,k,l=1}^{\ensuremath{d}} \mathrm{Tr}\parenth{Q_t^a E_{ij} Q_t^{q-2-a} E_{kl}} d\brackets{Q_{ij}, Q_{kl}}_t, \end{align} where $E_{ij}$ is the matrix that takes $1$ at the entry $(i, j)$ and $0$ otherwise and $Q_{ij, t}$ is the stochastic process defined by the $(i,j)$ entry of $Q_t$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives

nodes.name: Plug in $dQ_t$ and its covariation
nodes.statement: Using the derivative of $A_t$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:known_SDE_change_At}, we have \begin{align*} dQ_t &= \int A^{-1/2} \parenth{x - \mu_t} \parenth{x - \mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} \parenth{\parenth{x-\mu_t}^\top A^{-1/2} dW_t} p_t(x) dx - Q_t^2 dt, \\ d\brackets{Q_{ij}, Q_{kl}}_t &= \int \int z(x)_i z(x)_j z(y)_k z(y)_l (x-\mu_t)^\top A^{-1} (y-\mu_t) p_t(x) p_t(y)dx dy dt, \end{align*} where $z(x)_i$ is the $i$-th coordinate of $\brackets{A^{-1/2}(x-\mu_t)}$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3 and derivatives
